meta.title: Romanian A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Romanian → English (see the Romanian, recall the meaning) and English → Romanian (see an English meaning, recall the Romanian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be — no openly licensed graded word list for Romanian was found to build it from. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 354 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and conjunctions every sentence is built out of — and the other 146 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Romanian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword carries its pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, Wiktionary's own, because Romanian does not write where the stress falls. Verbs are given in the dictionary's form, with the infinitive's a (a face, to do). The 192 nouns show their gender — masculine, feminine or neuter, the neuter being masculine in the singular and feminine in the plural — their plural, and their definite form, the article being a suffix (casă, a house; casa, the house); the 100 verbs show their first person, past participle and subjunctive, and behind the All forms fold their present, imperfect, subjunctive and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 498 of the 500 words, three apiece for 495 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
